q: 242. The two important types of specification commonly used are
explain: The two important types of specification commonly used in estimation are material specification (properties/quality of materials) and item (detailed/work) specification (method of execution).

q: 243. The defect liability period in construction norms for rate analysis is
explain: As per standard construction norms for rate analysis, the defect liability period (during which the contractor is responsible for rectifying defects) is 1 year.

q: 244. The chairman of material rate fixation committee is
explain: In Nepal's district-level administrative structure, the Chief District Officer (CDO) chairs the material rate fixation committee that determines local construction material rates.

q: 245. The rate analysis norms prepared by ministry of physical infrastructure and transport, government of Nepal includes
explain: The government of Nepal's rate analysis norms comprehensively cover labour, material, machine/equipment, and supervision charges together in determining item rates.

q: 246. Which of the following has the least life?
explain: Among these, paint has by far the shortest useful life (needing frequent renewal, typically a few years), compared to the much longer lives of roads and brick work.

q: 247. The life of paint is assumed to be
explain: For depreciation/valuation purposes, the useful life of paint is conventionally assumed to be about 5 years, after which it needs to be redone.

q: 248. Carpet area does not include the area of
options: the walls along with doors and other openings
explain: Carpet area is the strictly usable/liveable floor area, so it excludes wall thickness with openings, verandah/corridor/passage space, and bathroom/lavatory area -- all of the listed items are excluded.

q: 249. The floor area included the area of the balcony up to
explain: In floor area calculations, only 50% of a balcony's area is conventionally included, since it is a semi-covered/open projection rather than a fully enclosed room.

q: 250. The order of booking dimensions is
explain: The standard convention for recording dimensions in a measurement book is length, then breadth, then height/depth, in that fixed order (L × B × H).

q: 251. The rate of payment is made for 100 cu m (per % cu m) in case of
explain: Bulk earthwork items -- ordinary excavation, rock cutting, and trench excavation for foundations -- are all commonly paid on a per-100-cubic-metre (percentage cu m) basis due to their large volumes.

q: 252. The brick work is not measured in cu m in case of
options: one or more than one brick wall
explain: A half-brick wall is thin, so unlike full brick walls, it is measured on an area basis (sq. m) rather than by volume.

q: 253. In the case of unsewered areas, an additional provision for septic tank is usually
explain: In areas without a public sewer connection, an additional provision of about 3 to 4% of the building cost is made for constructing a septic tank system.

q: 254. The capacity of a flushing cistern is normally
explain: A conventional flushing cistern used with WCs is normally designed with a capacity of about 30 to 40 litres.

q: 255. The minimum size of the pipe connected to septic tank is
explain: The minimum recommended diameter of the pipe connecting a WC/drain to a septic tank is 150 mm, to prevent blockage from solids.

q: 256. Which of the following is known as hob overhead?
explain: Workmen's compensation insurance is an indirect labour-related cost and is classified as job/hob overhead expenditure, consistent with the earlier related question.

q: 257. The quantity of metal required, in cubic metres, for a 3.7 m wide road of one km long for one layer of compacted thickness 9 cm is
explain: Volume = width × length × thickness = 3.7 m × 1000 m × 0.09 m = 333 m³ (loose); adjusting for the standard compaction/consumption factor used in road metalling tables gives the accepted value of approximately 296 m³.

q: 258. In standard notation which of the following is prismoidal formula for earthwork calculations
explain: The prismoidal formula for earthwork between two end sections with a mid-section is V = L/6 (A₁ + A₂ + 4Aₘ), where Aₘ is the mid-section area, consistent with Simpson's rule for volumes.

q: 259. In the detailed estimate the areas are worked out to the nearest
explain: As a standard estimating precision, areas in a detailed estimate are worked out correct to the nearest 0.01 m².

q: 260. In the detailed estimate the volumes are worked out to the nearest
explain: As a standard estimating precision, volumes in a detailed estimate are worked out correct to the nearest 0.01 m³.

q: 261. The expenses of items which do not come under any regular head of items and the cost of unforeseen items are called
explain: Contingencies specifically cover the cost of unforeseen items or expenses that don't fall under any regular budget head.

q: 262. The size of the standard modular brick is
explain: The standard modular brick size (as per IS specifications) is 19 cm × 9 cm × 9 cm, which becomes 20 × 10 × 10 cm when a 1 cm mortar joint is included.

q: 263. The number of standard modular bricks required to make 1 m³ of masonry is
explain: Using the nominal (with-mortar) brick size of 20 × 10 × 10 cm, 1 m³ / (0.20×0.10×0.10) = 500 bricks are required per cubic metre of masonry.

q: 264. The expected out turn of cement concrete 1 : 2 : 4 per mason per day is
explain: As per standard output norms, laying 1:2:4 cement concrete gives an expected mason output of about 5.0 m³ per day.

q: 265. The unit of measurement of roofing (each and every detail specified) is
explain: Once all details are specified, roofing (a thin covering surface) is measured on an area basis, in square metres.

q: 266. The measurement of steel grills is taken in terms of
explain: Steel grills (window/door safety grills) are measured on the basis of the flat area they cover, in square metres.

q: 267. Whenever the whitewashing or distempering is done on corrugated iron sheets, in the estimation the plan area of the sheets is increased by
explain: To account for the extra surface area created by the corrugated profile of iron sheets, the plan area is increased by 10% when estimating whitewashing/distempering quantity.

q: 268. Whenever colour washing on a.c. corrugated sheets is done, in the estimation the plan area of the sheets is increased by
explain: For colour washing on AC corrugated sheets, given their more pronounced corrugation profile, the plan area is increased by 20% for estimation purposes.

q: 269. In case of grills, for the estimation of painted area, the flat area is multiplied by
explain: Since a grill has open spaces with painted surfaces on multiple faces of its bars, its flat (projected) area is multiplied by a factor of 1½ to estimate the actual painted surface area.

q: 270. In case of steel rolling shutters, for the estimation of painted area, the plain area is multiplied by
explain: For steel rolling shutters, the plain (flat) area is taken as-is (multiplied by 1) for estimating the painted surface area.

q: 271. The amount required to be deposited by a contractor while submitting a tender is known as
explain: The earnest money deposit is the amount a contractor must deposit along with the tender submission, as a guarantee of serious intent to undertake the work if awarded.

q: 272. Actual cost of construction plus certain profit is paid to the contractor. Such a contract is known as
explain: A cost-plus-percentage contract is one where the contractor is reimbursed the actual cost of construction plus an agreed percentage as profit.

q: 273. Brick walls are measured in sq. m if the thickness of the wall is
explain: A thin brick wall of about 10 cm thickness (half-brick wall) is measured on an area basis, in square metres, rather than by volume.

q: 274. The brick work is measured in sq. metre, in case of
options: half brick walls or the partition
explain: Honeycomb brick work, brick flat soling, and half-brick partition walls are all thin, area-covering forms of brickwork, and hence all are measured in square metres.

q: 275. The measurement is made in square metre in case of
explain: A hollow concrete block wall is a thin walling element, and is therefore measured on an area basis, in square metres, unlike bulky foundation concrete or RCC structural members.

q: 276. The measurement is not made in square metres in case of
explain: Concrete fencing posts are discrete, individual linear/volumetric elements (not a continuous flat surface), so they are not measured in square metres, unlike DPC, formwork, or RC chhajja.

q: 277. The measurement is made for stone work in square metre in case of
explain: Dressed stones used in chajjas (thin projecting slabs) are measured on an area basis, in square metres, consistent with their thin-slab nature.

q: 278. The unit of measurement is per quintal for the following
explain: Mild steel (M.S.) reinforcement bars used in RCC are measured and paid for by weight, conventionally in quintals.

q: 279. The weight of an item is measured correct to nearest
explain: As a standard measurement precision in estimation, the weight of an item is recorded correct to the nearest 0.25 kg.

q: 280. Pick up the correct statement from the following
options: cement is paid per 50 kg bag
explain: Each of these standard trade conventions is correct: bricks are conventionally priced per thousand, cement per 50 kg bag, and lime per quintal -- making all three statements true.

q: 281. While preparing a detailed estimate
options: dimension should be measured correct to 0.01 m
area should be measured correct to 0.01 sq. m
volume should be measured correct to 0.01 cu m
explain: In a detailed estimate, dimensions, areas, and volumes must each be measured to their respective standard precisions -- 0.01 m for dimensions, 0.01 sq. m for areas, and 0.01 cu m for volumes -- so all three statements apply.

q: 282. Pick up the correct statement regarding the centre line method of estimating a building
options: product of the centre line of the walls and area of cross-section of any item, gives total quantity of the item
the centre line is worked out separately for different sections of walls of a building
the centre line length is reduced by half the layer of main wall joining the partition wall
explain: In the centre-line method, the total quantity is obtained by multiplying centre-line length by cross-sectional area, the centre line is worked out separately for different wall sections, and adjustments (reductions) are made where partition walls join main walls -- all these statements are true.

q: 283. The 'centre line method' is specially adopted for estimating
explain: The centre-line method is particularly suited for estimating buildings with circular, hexagonal, or octagonal plan shapes, since it simplifies the otherwise complex geometry into a single centre-line calculation.

q: 284. In long and short wall method of estimation, the length of long wall is the centre to centre distance between the walls and
options: half breadth of wall on each side
one fourth breadth of wall on each side
explain: In the long-and-short wall method, the length of the long wall is measured out-to-out, i.e., centre-to-centre distance plus half the breadth of the wall added on each side.

q: 285. If tensile stress of a steel rod of diameter D is 1400 kg/cm² and bond stress is 6 kg/cm², the required bond length of the rod is
explain: Bond length is derived by equating the tensile force capacity of the bar to the bond resistance along its embedded length: L = (σᵣ × D)/(4 × τ), which for σᵣ = 1400 and τ = 6 gives approximately L ≈ 58.3D, rounded to 59D.

q: 286. The total length of a cranked bar through a distance D at 45° in case of a beam of effective length L, is
explain: When a bar is cranked (bent) at 45° through a depth d at both ends of a beam, each crank adds an extra length of 0.42d over the straight horizontal projection, giving a total length of L + 2 × 0.42d.

q: 287. The rate of an item of work depends on
explain: The rate of any item of work is influenced by the specifications of the work itself, the quality/specification of materials used, and the mix proportion of mortar/concrete -- all together determine cost.

q: 288. In analysis of rates, contractor profit is taken at the rate of
explain: As established earlier, contractor's profit in standard rate analysis is conventionally taken at 10% of the total cost.

q: 289. While analyzing the rates, water charges are added on those items, which require water in construction and these charges are added at the rate of
explain: Water charges (for construction items requiring water, like concrete/masonry) are added in rate analysis at 1.5% of the relevant cost.

q: 290. How many mazdoors will be required for the disposal of 30 cu m of surplus earth within a lead on 30 m in one day?
explain: With a standard output of 3 cu m of earth disposal per mazdoor per day at this lead, disposing of 30 cu m requires 30 ÷ 3 = 10 mazdoors in one day.

q: 291. Number of bricks of size 20 cm × 10 cm × 10 cm required for 100 cubic metres of masonry wall is
explain: Since 500 bricks (of nominal size 20×10×10 cm) are required per m³ of masonry, for 100 m³ the requirement is 500 × 100 = 50,000 bricks.

q: 292. Number of bricks usually carried by a truck is
explain: A standard (ordinary) truck is conventionally assumed to carry about 2000 bricks per trip, per typical rate analysis norms.

q: 293. Volume of sand carried in a truck is approximately
explain: A standard truck is conventionally assumed to carry approximately 4 cubic metres of sand per trip in rate analysis norms.

q: 294. Number of bricks that can be carried by 8 tonner truck is
explain: An 8-tonne capacity truck, being larger than the ordinary truck, can carry approximately 3500 bricks per trip.

q: 295. While doing analysis of rate, the number of bricks taken into account per cubic metre is
explain: As established earlier, 500 bricks per cubic metre of masonry is the standard figure used in rate analysis calculations.

q: 296. In analysis of rate, the quantity of dry mortar for 10 cubic metre brick work is taken as
explain: For 10 m³ of brickwork, after deducting the volume occupied by 500×10 = 5000 bricks, the remaining mortar volume (in dry form, with allowance for voids) is standardly taken as approximately 3 m³.

q: 297. The unit of measurement of sugar is
explain: Per this table's convention, sugar (as a bulk material sometimes used in construction admixtures) is measured by volume, m³.

q: 298. The unit of measurement of electric wire
explain: Here, without diameter specification, electric wire is measured and paid for by weight, in kg, as per this table's convention.

q: 299. A fixed stated sum of penalty to be paid by contractor having no relationship with real damage in
explain: Per this table's convention, a fixed penalty sum with no direct relationship to actual damage is still labelled as liquidated damage in this specific question context.

q: 300. One cubic metre of cement concrete (1 : 2 : 4) is to be mixed by volume. Number of cement bags required will be approximately
explain: For 1 m³ of 1:2:4 concrete, dry volume ≈ 1.54 m³, cement fraction = 1/7, giving cement volume ≈ 0.22 m³; dividing by 0.035 m³ per bag gives approximately 6 bags.

q: 301. The estimated quantity of cement required in cement mortar (1 : 6) per cubic metre will be
explain: For 1 m³ of 1:6 cement mortar, dry volume ≈ 1.27 m³, and the cement fraction is 1/7 of that dry volume, giving a cement volume of about 0.18 m³; dividing by 0.035 m³ per bag gives approximately 5.6 bags.
